structured_output.hypothesis: In a sample of Norway spruce (Picea abies) cones with a 5:8 parastichy arrangement, the proportion with right-handed five-series is statistically indistinguishable from 0.5.
structured_output.pass_criterion: With at least 300 scored cones of one species and one parastichy arrangement, a two-sided exact binomial test against p=0.5 gives p>=0.05, and the right-handed share lies within 0.45-0.55 (Thompson's own 224/467 = 0.48 would pass).
structured_output.fail_criterion: The two-sided exact binomial test gives p<0.01 and the right-handed share falls outside 0.40-0.60 in a pooled sample of at least 300 cones, meaning a strong handedness bias.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Right-/left-handed direction' of the 5-series maps to a recorded chirality (clockwise vs counter-clockwise) of the parastichy family with the lower count, per cone, scored with a stated viewing convention. This is the modern 'phyllotactic chirality'. The claim is specific to cones within a species and a given parastichy arrangement, so shoot or leaf chirality data would not test it.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: Two searches found no public dataset recording per-cone parastichy chirality for Norway spruce or any other conifer. The hits were journal articles on calathea, lodgepole pine shoots and larch cone parastichy counts, and none was a deposited per-cone chirality table for the species and structure Thompson names. I fetched no landing page, so I am not naming one. Shoot or leaf chirality sets would test a different claim.
